topics.title: Lecture Framing and the Memory Wall

notes.title: Course Framing and the Central Memory Question
notes.summary: 本讲的核心问题是：如何设计内存系统以充分利用现代CPU/GPU，尤其是在AI时代。
notes.detail: 课程从回顾冯·诺依曼架构出发，指出性能受数据供给限制，即内存墙；随后对比CPU与GPU内存子系统，并讨论内存技术演进。
keyPoints: 核心问题：如何设计内存系统以充分利用现代CPU/GPU，尤其是AI时代
路径：回顾冯·诺依曼架构→内存墙→CPU vs GPU内存子系统→内存技术演进
冯·诺依曼架构将内存与处理单元分离，形成内存墙瓶颈
PU执行指令比内存访问快数个数量级

notes.title: The Main Memory System Across Platforms
notes.summary: 主存是所有计算系统的关键组件，存储保留程序与数据，主存保存可活跃执行的部分，缓存减少从主存的传输。
notes.detail: 在FPGA上，片上SRAM（如block RAM）在处理逻辑附近缓冲输入和中间结果；独立GPU使用自己的设备DRAM（GDDR或HBM堆栈），结果可留在设备内存供下次计算或返回CPU内存。
keyPoints: 主存是服务器、移动、嵌入式、桌面、传感器等所有计算系统的关键组件
存储跨运行保留程序和数据，主存保存可供活跃执行的部分
缓存将副本保持在执行单元附近，减少从主存的传输
FPGA用片上SRAM（block RAM）缓冲输入和中间结果
独立GPU使用GDDR或HBM设备DRAM，结果可留在设备内存或返回CPU内存

notes.title: The Processor-DRAM Performance Gap and Scaling Laws
notes.summary: 处理器-DRAM性能差距历史上每年扩大50%，更快的处理器本身并不保证更快的应用。
notes.detail: LLM缩放定律带来参数、数据、思维链长度和搜索深度的增加；AI加速器的后Dennard缩放使Tensor Core吞吐增长远快于HBM容量，从而加宽内存墙。
keyPoints: 处理器-DRAM性能差距每年增长50%（该图的历史时期）
更快的处理器本身不保证更快的应用
LLM缩放定律：参数和数据量增加，思维链长度和搜索深度增加
Tensor Core吞吐增长远快于HBM容量，加宽内存墙

notes.title: Memory Wall: Capacity, Bandwidth, and Latency
notes.summary: 内存墙体现在容量、带宽和延迟三个维度，核心数增长快于DRAM容量导致每核内存容量下降。
notes.detail: PU核心数约每2年翻倍，而DRAM DIMM容量约每3年翻倍，预计每核内存容量每两年下降30%，大量数据可能需从低速磁盘加载；带宽和延迟趋势也在恶化，内存性能通常是整个系统的瓶颈。
keyPoints: PU核心数约每2年翻倍，DRAM DIMM容量约每3年翻倍
每核内存容量预计每两年下降30%
大量数据可能从低速磁盘加载
带宽和延迟趋势恶化

topics.title: Modern Memory Systems and Cache Hierarchy

notes.title: High-Level Structure of Modern Memory Systems
notes.summary: Modern memory systems are organized as a hierarchy in which registers and caches sit near the processor to reduce how often execution depends on slower main memory.
notes.detail: Registers and caches reduce how often execution depends on slower main memory. Data reuse near the processor reduces traffic across the memory hierarchy.
keyPoints: Registers and caches reduce dependence on slower main memory.
Data reuse near the processor reduces traffic across the memory hierarchy.
The page presents this only at a high level, without detailing the individual hierarchy levels.

notes.title: Deeper and Larger Cache Hierarchies in Real Processors
notes.summary: Real processors have evolved toward deeper and larger cache hierarchies, with private caches near each core and shared caches for reuse across the processor.
notes.detail: AMD Barcelona (2007) exemplifies this with private caches keeping frequently used data near each core and a shared cache supporting reuse across the processor. Later processors like AMD Ryzen 5000 and IBM POWER10 increase cache capacity (e.g., 32MB or 120MB shared L3) to reduce traffic to main memory, while access time still depends on data location.
keyPoints: Private caches keep frequently used data near each core.
A shared cache supports reuse across the processor.
Cache capacity helps reduce traffic to main memory.
Access time still depends on the location of the data.

notes.title: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
notes.summary: The memory hierarchy exploits temporal and spatial locality by using fast, small, expensive memory for frequent data and slow, large, cheap memory for less frequent data.
notes.detail: Temporal locality means a piece of data is quickly reused in the future (e.g., loops), while spatial locality means neighbors of the current access tend to be accessed soon (e.g., arrays). High-speed caches capture these localities to address the memory wall, and the hierarchy is useful when a small, active subset of the working set receives most accesses.
keyPoints: For frequent data: use fast but expensive and small memory (e.g., cache).
For not frequent data: use slow but cheap and large memory (e.g., main memory, disk).
Temporal locality: data is quickly reused in the future, e.g., loops.
Spatial locality: neighbors of current access tend to be accessed in the future, e.g., arrays.
Capture localities with high-speed caches to address memory wall.

notes.title: Cache Hits, Misses, and Average Memory Access Time
notes.summary: A hit means the requested block is found in the current cache level with a valid tag match; a miss means it must be fetched from the next lower level, and AMAT combines hit time with the cost of misses.
notes.detail: AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty, where miss penalty is the time to fetch a block from a lower memory level (access time plus data size / bandwidth). A cache helps only when common hits stay fast and sufficiently few accesses pay the miss penalty.
keyPoints: Hit rate = Hits / Total Accesses; miss rate = 1 − Hit rate.
Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth.
Example: 1-cycle hit, 10% miss rate, 300-cycle penalty gives AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × 300 = 31 cycles.
A cache helps when common hits remain fast and sufficiently few accesses pay the miss penalty.
notes.formula: \(AMAT = Hit\ time + Miss\ rate \times Miss\ penalty\)

notes.title: Reducing Miss Penalty: Multi-Level Caches and Code Optimization
notes.summary: Multi-level caches (L1/L2/L3) shorten the effective miss penalty by nesting faster levels before DRAM, and blocking/tiling improves locality so fewer accesses miss.
notes.detail: The nested AMAT formula adds each level's hit time and only charges the next level's cost on a miss: Thit(L1) + Miss%(L1)×(Thit(L2) + Miss%(L2)×(Thit(L3) + Miss%(L3)×T(memory))). Code optimization replaces poor-locality column-wise traversal with blocking/tiling that computes on B×B tiles.
keyPoints: Level latencies shown: L1 1 clk, L2 10 clks, L3 20 clks, main memory 300 clks.
L2 and L3 sit on-die between L1 and DRAM.
Poor locality: column-wise traversal of A[i][j].
Better locality: blocking/tiling with compute_tile over B×B blocks.

notes.title: End-to-End Load/Store Path
notes.summary: A load/store flows through address resolution, the TLB, the cache hierarchy, and DRAM, with TLB and cache misses triggering different recovery work.
notes.detail: A TLB miss requires address translation work, while a cache miss determines whether the data must come from a lower level. Only a miss through the cache hierarchy sends the data request to the memory controller and DRAM.
keyPoints: A TLB miss requires address translation work.
A cache miss determines whether data must come from a lower level.
Only a miss through the cache hierarchy reaches the memory controller and DRAM.

notes.title: SRAM vs. DRAM
notes.summary: SRAM stores bits in stable transistor circuits (6 transistors/bit, low power, used in caches and register files), while DRAM stores bits as charge on tiny capacitors (1 transistor/bit, cheap, needs rewriting and refresh, used in DDR/GDDR/HBM).
notes.detail: SRAM reads precharge bit and bitbar to Vdd, select the row, let the cell pull one line, and use a sense amp to detect the difference; DRAM reads precharge the bit line, share charge between cell and bit line, and sense very small voltage changes (~10–100k electrons), restoring the value on write. DRAM addresses are multiplexed with RAS for the upper half and CAS for the lower half.
keyPoints: SRAM: 6 transistors/bit, expensive, retains bit with low power (423mV for 45nm).
DRAM: 1 transistor/bit, cheap, must be re-written after read and periodically refreshed (each row simultaneously).
DRAM address lines are multiplexed: RAS = upper half, CAS = lower half.
Usage: SRAM in caches and register files; DRAM in DDR/GDDR/HBM.

notes.title: DRAM Refresh and Why DRAM Is Slow
notes.summary: DRAM stores bits as leaky capacitor charges, so every row must be periodically refreshed, making it briefly inaccessible and consuming refresh time.
notes.detail: With 4K rows and a 100ns read cycle, refreshing all rows once takes about 410µs, which is roughly 0.64% of the 64ms refresh window. DRAM is also slow because the weak storage signal must be sensed and amplified, reads are destructive and require restore, and the arrays are large and dense.
keyPoints: Each row is un-accessible while it is being refreshed.
Refresh overhead is about 410µs / 64ms = 0.64%.
Weak capacitor charge produces only a small voltage difference on long bitlines.
Sense amplifiers need time to detect and amplify the tiny voltage change.
A read disturbs the stored charge, so data must be restored after every row activation.

notes.title: DRAM Organization: Banks, Ranks, Controller, and Channels
notes.summary: DRAM is organized as banks inside chips, chips grouped into ranks, ranks sharing a channel driven by a memory controller, giving independent storage arrays but a shared data bus.
notes.detail: Banks are independent storage arrays, so work in one bank can overlap preparation in another, but the shared data bus still limits how much data the channel can return at once. A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width, and multiple ranks share the channel while the controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.
keyPoints: Banks provide independent storage arrays; work in one bank can overlap preparation in another.
The shared data bus limits how much data the channel can return at once.
A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width; multiple ranks share the channel.
The controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.
One memory-controller port drives one channel; all ranks share the data bus and only the selected rank may drive it.

notes.title: DRAM Generations: DDR1 to DDR5
notes.summary: From DDR1 to DDR5, aggregate x64 bandwidth rises from 3.2 to 51.2 GB/s at the selected upper rates, driven mainly by faster interfaces rather than faster cells.
notes.detail: Faster interfaces, longer bursts, and more bank parallelism raise throughput, while cell access improves more slowly. This widening gap between interface speed and cell speed is the core of the DRAM bandwidth story across generations.
keyPoints: Same aggregate x64 width rises from 3.2 to 51.2 GB/s.
Faster interfaces raise throughput.
Longer bursts raise throughput.
More bank parallelism raises throughput.
Cell access improves more slowly than the interface.

notes.title: GPU Memory Spaces and the GPU Memory Wall
notes.summary: The GPU memory lecture covers CUDA memory spaces and access patterns plus GDDR and HBM, framing the GPU memory wall alongside the CPU memory wall.
notes.detail: The page is a section title slide, so it only names the topics: CUDA memory spaces and access patterns, and GDDR and HBM. It does not itself explain how the GPU memory wall differs from the CPU memory wall.
keyPoints: Topics named: CUDA memory spaces and access patterns.
Topics named: GDDR and HBM.
The GPU memory wall is presented alongside the CPU memory wall.
The page gives no explicit comparison of the two walls.

notes.title: GPU Memory Hierarchy: Capacity vs. Access Time
notes.summary: GPU storage levels trade capacity against access time: per-thread registers, per-SM shared memory plus L1, device-wide L2, and off-chip GDDR/HBM device memory.
notes.detail: Registers are allocated per thread and hardware managed, while shared memory is a per-SM explicit scratchpad and L1 is a hardware cache. L2 is device-wide and shared by all SMs, and device memory (GDDR/HBM) is off-chip physical memory serving the global address space.
keyPoints: Registers: allocated per thread, hardware managed.
Shared memory + L1: per-SM explicit scratchpad plus hardware cache.
L2 cache: device-wide, shared by all SMs.
Device memory: GDDR/HBM off-chip, serving the global address space.
Larger capacity comes with longer access time.

notes.title: GPU Memory Access Path and CUDA Memory Model
notes.summary: A GPU memory access passes through SM-local storage and the shared L2 before reaching device DRAM, while CUDA memory spaces are defined by scope and lifetime and map to physical resources.
notes.detail: A request reaches device-wide L2 through the on-chip interconnect, and an L2 miss continues to a memory controller; all SMs share L2 and the DRAM partitions, implemented with GDDR devices or HBM channels. Programmer-side, scope identifies which threads can access data and lifetime identifies how long the data exists, with each CUDA memory space mapping to a physical resource.
keyPoints: L2 is device-wide and shared by all SMs, as are the DRAM partitions.
An L2 miss continues to a memory controller.
__syncthreads() coordinates threads within one block but does not synchronize different blocks.
Local memory is thread-private in scope but usually resides in device DRAM and passes through L1/L2.
Register and shared-memory allocations limit how many blocks and warps can reside on an SM.

notes.title: Warp Memory Access and Coalescing
notes.summary: A single warp memory instruction can generate up to 32 addresses, which the coalescer groups by cache-sector or transaction granularity before DRAM access.
notes.detail: Coalescing is evaluated per warp memory instruction: aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments, while misalignment crosses extra boundaries and strided accesses touch many more segments. The resulting transaction count depends on alignment, address spacing, access width, and GPU architecture.
keyPoints: The coalescer groups addresses by cache-sector or transaction granularity before DRAM access.
Transaction count depends on alignment, address spacing, access width, and GPU architecture.
Aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments.
Misalignment can cross extra boundaries; strided accesses can touch many more segments.

notes.title: Data Layout and Shared Memory Staging
notes.summary: Row-wise and column-wise traversal can do the same arithmetic but transfer different byte counts, so useful bandwidth depends on requested versus actually transferred bytes.
notes.detail: Software explicitly chooses which data to stage in shared memory and when threads must synchronize. One off-chip load can then support repeated on-chip reuse, reducing DRAM traffic and increasing arithmetic intensity.
keyPoints: Row-wise and column-wise traversal perform the same arithmetic while transferring different byte counts.
Useful bandwidth depends on requested bytes relative to bytes actually transferred.
Software explicitly chooses the data to stage in shared memory and when threads synchronize.
One off-chip load can support repeated on-chip reuse, reducing DRAM traffic and raising arithmetic intensity.

notes.title: Shared Memory Bank Conflicts
notes.summary: Different addresses in the same shared-memory bank require multiple service rounds, serializing accesses that would otherwise be parallel.
notes.detail: Typical GPUs use 32 banks (the figure shows 8 for readability). Same-address reads can use broadcast, and bank conflicts differ from global-memory coalescing.
keyPoints: Typical GPUs use 32 banks; the figure shows 8 for readability.
Same-address reads can use broadcast.
Different addresses in the same bank require multiple service rounds.
Bank conflicts differ from global-memory coalescing.

notes.title: From DDR DIMMs to GDDR
notes.summary: GDDR replaces socketed DDR DIMMs with soldered devices on short point-to-point links, trading expandability for higher per-pin data rates.
notes.detail: Aggregate bandwidth is the sum across independent memory-controller channels, but more channels, wider buses, and faster signaling also raise pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power. GDDR6X uses PAM4 as a vendor extension, while GDDR7 uses PAM3 and further divides the channels.
keyPoints: Socketed DIMMs use multiple ranks, replaceable modules, and longer routed channels.
GDDR uses soldered devices and short point-to-point links, permitting higher per-pin data rates with less expandability.
Aggregate bandwidth is the sum across independent memory-controller channels.
More channels, wider buses, and faster signaling raise pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power.
GDDR6X uses PAM4 as a vendor extension; GDDR7 uses PAM3 and further divides the channels.

notes.title: From GDDR to HBM
notes.summary: HBM uses thousands of short wires, stacked dies, and 2.5D packaging to deliver high bandwidth and energy efficiency per bit.
notes.detail: HBM1–HBM3 use a 1024-bit interface per stack, and HBM4 expands this to 2048 bits. TSVs carry signals and power through the stack, micro-bumps connect adjacent dies, and HBM commonly sits beside the XPU on an interposer.
keyPoints: HBM1–HBM3 use a 1024-bit interface per stack; HBM4 expands to 2048 bits.
TSVs carry signals and power through the stack; micro-bumps connect adjacent dies.
More stacked dies increase capacity; wide channel organization increases bandwidth.
HBM commonly sits beside the XPU on an interposer, forming a 2.5D package.
Dense, short wiring improves bandwidth and energy per bit but requires advanced packaging, with costs in assembly, yield, cooling, and power delivery.

notes.title: DDR, GDDR, and HBM Tradeoffs
notes.summary: DDR, GDDR, and HBM optimize different constraints, so the right choice depends on the workload and system constraints.
notes.detail: DDR favors capacity, expandability, and cost per GB; GDDR balances pin bandwidth and board cost; HBM favors bandwidth per package and per watt.
keyPoints: DDR favors capacity, expandability, and cost per GB.
GDDR balances pin bandwidth and board cost.
HBM favors bandwidth per package and per watt.
The choice depends on the workload and system constraints.

notes.title: Shared LLC in Multicore Processors
notes.summary: A banked LLC is logically shared across cores but physically distributed, with a physical-address hash selecting a home slice so that only the first cold read must reach DRAM.
notes.detail: Remote-slice reads and writes would slow memory access speed, so the hash-based home-slice mapping keeps accesses local where possible. A second reader can obtain the line from the LLC or its current owner instead of DRAM.
keyPoints: Physical-address hash selects a home LLC slice
Reads/writes to remote slices slow memory access
Only the first cold read must reach DRAM
A second reader gets the line from the LLC or current owner
Simplified inclusive teaching model; modern LLCs may be non-inclusive

notes.title: Cache Coherence and Coherence Protocols
notes.summary: Coherence is needed because a write can make another core's copy stale, requiring write propagation and write serialization across processors.
notes.detail: Snooping broadcasts coherence requests, while a directory tracks owners and sharers to target messages; MESI describes permissions, and the protocol design determines how coherence messages reach the caches.
keyPoints: A write can make another core's copy stale
Write propagation: others must eventually observe the write
Write serialization: all processors agree on one order for writes to the same location
Snooping broadcasts requests; a directory tracks owners and sharers
MESI describes permissions, not message routing

notes.title: Capacity Wall of LLM Inference: DeepSeek Case Study
notes.summary: KV-cache size grows with context length, so on a GB200 GPU with ~150GB of HBM available for KV-cache, the maximum number of sessions is bounded by cache capacity.
notes.detail: The case study compares approximate session KV-cache sizes for DeepSeek v3.2 and DeepSeek v4 (with CSA/HCA/SWA) at 128K context length, showing how context length drives capacity limits.
keyPoints: Available HBM capacity for KV-cache is ~150GB on GB200
At 128K context, DeepSeek v3.2 needs ~5.72 GiB per session
DeepSeek v4 with CSA/HCA/SWA needs ~0.62 GiB per session
Context length directly scales KV-cache size

notes.title: Memory Extension with CXL
notes.summary: CXL extends host memory through a unified host address map spanning host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM, with hardware translating load/store instructions into CXL remote memory accesses.
notes.detail: Software sees host-memory ranges while hardware handles translation to CXL remote memory. CXL switches enable expansion (capacity for one host), pooling (portions of devices assigned to different hosts), and coherent sharing in CXL 3.0.
keyPoints: Unified memory across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM
Software sees host-memory ranges; hardware translates accesses
Expansion adds capacity to one host
Pooling assigns portions of memory devices to different hosts
CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from merely mapping the same region

notes.title: Memory Extension with LPDDR
notes.summary: In Grace-Hopper, Hopper retains local HBM while Grace connects LPDDR5X through the coherent NVLink-C2C CPU–GPU link, extending the capacity the accelerator can address.
notes.detail: LPDDR extends addressable capacity for the accelerator but does not enlarge HBM itself; the coherent link lets the GPU access the CPU-attached LPDDR tier.
keyPoints: Hopper retains local HBM
Grace connects LPDDR5X via coherent NVLink-C2C
LPDDR extends capacity the accelerator can address
LPDDR does not enlarge HBM itself

notes.title: Tiered Memory Management
notes.summary: Tiered memory management keeps hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM and places large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.
notes.detail: Promotion of data into HBM helps only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and bookkeeping cost, so placement is governed by reuse versus migration overhead.
keyPoints: Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM
Place large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier
Promotion pays off only if future reuse exceeds transfer and bookkeeping cost
